en: In the *Sūtra on the Exquisite and Wondrous Jeweled Chariot* spoken by the Buddha, at one time there was a bodhisattva who said: "As for all the myriad people..."
Do all prisoners in jail long to escape?
Do all the sick long to be cured?
Is it not as if a person in darkness longs to see light?
Is it not like a compassionate mother longing to see her child?
Is it not like one traveling afar longing to return home early?
Is it not like a widowed woman longing to find a husband?
It is like a person with crippled legs who longs to walk;
it is like a poor person who longs for clothing;
it is like a person suffering from cold who longs for fire.
Is it like plowing a field while hoping to obtain grain?
Is it like a blind person hoping to see objects?
Is it like a deaf person hoping to hear sounds?
It is like a mute person who longs to speak;
though they contemplate and reflect upon it in various ways,
the supreme path of the Buddha ultimately cannot be deceived.
The Buddha spoke to the Bodhisattva Ratnavāhana:
"I shall now tell you:
to the south of Mount Sumeru is the land named Jambudvīpa."
Aparagoyānī in the west,
Uttarakuru in the north,
and Pūrvavideha in the east.
Thus all sentient beings in the four directions hear and know it;
those who wish to hear it are like subjects who have obtained a king.
Like a prisoner released from jail;
like one who has recovered from illness;
like seeing light in the darkness.
It is like a compassionate mother who has found her child;
like a traveler from afar who has found his home;
like a widowed woman who has found a husband.
It is like a person who has gained the ability to walk;
it is like a poor person who has obtained clothing;
it is like a person suffering from cold who has found fire.
It is like a plowman obtaining grain;
it is like a blind person regaining sight;
it is like a deaf person regaining hearing.
It is as if a mute person has regained the power of speech;
such are the various ways I have contemplated and reflected upon the Buddha-way.
The World-Honored One will never deceive us.
The Bodhisattva Ratiratha addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One, for how many years is the lifespan of the Tathāgata?
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Ratiratha:
My present lifespan is inconceivable;
majestic and sublime, it is of equal duration to the sun and moon.
Day and night, I circumambulate Mount Sumeru.
It ends and begins again;
it has neither beginning nor origin.
If you wish to hear more:
That matter is also difficult:
all dharmas are empty and non-existent; there is nothing that is eternally abiding, nor is there anything that undergoes extinction.
It is like east and west, as well as south and north;
it is neither blue nor red, nor white nor black.
It is comparable to an echo or a sound, which cannot be grasped.
"O Bodhisattva Later Precious Chariot,
you should now instruct all sentient beings so that they may universally receive and uphold the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts."
Through the ten wholesome deeds and the eight precepts of the fast,
they were reborn and all attained the stage of Srotāpanna and the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin.
The path of the non-returner (anāgāmin),
the path of the arhat,
and the fourfold equipment for the exhaustion of all outflows (āsrava).
The Bodhisattva Ratraratha addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One, even while the Tathāgata remains in the world, there are still many who harbor resentment and malice;
how much more so after his parinirvāṇa?"
Those who slander this sutra shall,
upon death, enter hell;
they will transmigrate within it without any prospect of release.
How painful, how painful!
The pain is beyond words.
I now take pity on you for having composed this sutra.
Just as a blind person does not see the sun and moon, it is not the fault of the sun and moon.
When one loves, one does not see that love; not seeing love, one suffers grief. Therefore, do not create attachment.
Enmity arises from past malice; from joy, attachment is born. Attachment can give rise to sorrow;
if one can sever the bonds of affection, sorrow and lamentation will not arise. From attachment and joy, enmity is born;
from attachment and joy, fear is born. One who understands the absence of the notion of craving—what cause for sorrow and what cause for fear?
The palaces of the devas are joyful, boundless and inexhaustible; one must surely be born there, having a beginning but no end.
Taking the good as the wholesome dharma, practicing the good is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Good conduct acts as the oxen that draw the carriage, carrying people into the hall of merit. Taking the evil as the unwholesome dharma—
Bound by the fetters of evil conduct, one who does not receive the precepts at the time of birth will enter hell upon death.
The chariot of the Three Refuges and Five Precepts is not like a tree in the mountains; having heard this Sūtra of the Precious Chariot, one does not enter hell after death.
Neither in the sky nor in the midst of the ocean, nor by entering into the crevices of mountain rocks, can one escape.
When it arrives, it cannot be avoided; inevitably, we shall be drawn together. A crimson cord binds my shoulders, a black rope ties my throat.
Where will they lead me? They shall send me to Mount Tai in the East, a high mountain of over ten thousand *zhang*.
There, severed from life, one hangs in utter suspension for tens of millions of years.
To return once more to the Yellow Springs—human life is like the morning dew; one’s name and life-span are not long-lasting.
Those who do not believe my words, look only at the luster of chiseled stone. Life is difficult; what is death any different?
Departing without crossing the bridge, one is terrified at the head of the five paths, stripped of both upper and lower garments.
In hand they grasp seven-foot staves, with iron hooks as sharp as thorns;
Suddenly the fire-chariots arrive, along with copper pillars and iron beds. The freezing ice severs human bones; at the gates of hell are the boiling cauldrons.
The judicial officials sit facing one another, while the clerks hold two chests, All together drafting the legal documents.
Questioning me about the calamities of birth—how can one know the way through every matter?
How can suffering and pain, so difficult to endure, be overcome, O God among Gods? Is there not a method for immortality?
Those who harbor resentment and attachment as if out of affection, claiming the self is eternal— such are the deluded people of the world; some do not believe in this sutra.
Just as an untrained ox drags a person here and there, The Three Refuges are like the linchpin of the chariot,
The Five Precepts are like the yoke, The Ten Wholesome Deeds form the body of the carriage, The Eight Precepts are the side-rails, A straight mind is the axle-tree,
The Threefold Knowledge is the hub and felloe, And the observance of the precepts is the linchpin.
Breaking the precepts is like the fenders of a chariot; Discernment is like the two ears; The hook-like mind is like the practice of seated meditation;
Skillful means are like the canopy; The Buddha-way acts as the hub, with spokes racing toward it from all sides;
The wise are like the netting of the chariot; The Dharma Master is the gateway against Māra.
Regressing like a *śveta* (white) ox, he repents and strikes the *śvetabhadra* (white-bright) ox.
Through diligent effort, he becomes a draft ox pulling a cart as far as the Brahma-heaven. In the various palaces of the Brahma-heaven, the radiance is entirely spontaneous;
like spring flowers in full bloom, their wondrous colors delight the hearts of all. Such are these merits.
Having heard the *Ratnavāhana Sūtra*, one realizes that the Buddha-way is higher than heaven and its merit more weighty than the treasures of the earth.
The Great Bodhisattva Ratnavāhana has instructed me to perform repentance. Those who are foolish and ignorant in this world do not believe in the *Ratnavāhana Sūtra*;
when they die, they fall into hell, and hungry ghosts will eventually come before them.
Dragged headlong toward the mountain of blades, The face is as pale as lips turned blue;
One sees not the light of sun or moon, But hears only the sound of spirits being beaten. Such are these various agonies— Deep and dark, how utterly obscure!
Having failed to receive the precepts when born, When the moment arrives, what can one plead? There are even birds with iron beaks.
Flying down, it alights upon both shoulders; Lowering its head, it pecks at the person’s tongue; Raising its head, it pecks at the pupils of the eyes.
In a previous life, this person Uttered foul abuse on days of fasting; Refusing to accept the teacher’s instruction, They failed to perform repentance before the Buddha.
Today they undergo this retribution; Knowing this, what more could one create?
The Buddha said:
"If there are sons or daughters of good family who,
on the day of the fast, can [perform this] before the Three Honored Ones."
Those who confess and repent, taking pleasure in their own transgressions, shall have their sins extinguished and blessings arise;
they will not pass through the mountains of knives and swords, the boiling cauldrons, or the burning charcoal,
nor will they undergo suffering in the three miserable realms.
If sentient beings do not encounter the eight difficulties,
they shall join hands and link arms with the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
they shall enter the celestial palaces and behold them all within, rejoicing with great joy and happiness.
Expounding his vast and great vows,
the Buddha spoke to the Bodhisattva Ratiratha:
"Should there be anyone capable of receiving and upholding this *Ratiratha-bodhisattva-sūtra*,"
Suppose they enter the great ocean;
like a female quail, a mandarin duck, a phoenix, and a peacock, they soar with wonder and grace amidst the waters of the sea.
It is as if a person in a hall were playing the lute, the zither, and the flute, performing songs and dances with joy and delight.
Their merit is immeasurable.
For example, it is like fish and turtles in the ocean who move in and out with ease, unafraid of tigers or wolves;
they are like those dwelling in deep seclusion, invisible spirits.
"Who dares? Who is fit?
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Ratnavāhana, "You should now instruct all sentient beings so that they may all hear and know it."
The Buddha said,
"As for the method by which you wish to deliver sentient beings,
what are its particulars?"
Ratnavāhana replied,
"One who is able to grasp with their hand the wisdom-torch of *prajñā* and enter the cave-dwelling of the ignorance of sentient beings."
It causes the flowers of the roots of goodness to bloom and manifests the fruit of wisdom of liberation;
it employs patience as armor and staff.
Holding the sharp blade of Prajñā in hand,
one employs skillful means as a siege engine to shatter the great fortress of sentient beings' ignorance.
They wage war against the demon of the five aggregates,
strike down the army of birth and death,
and slay the thieves of affliction.
The emergence from the aggregates, sense-bases,
and elements into the dharmakāya maṇḍala is entirely due to the majestic divine sword of the Bodhisattva Ratnaratha;
its loftiness is thus.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Ratnavāhana:
"Good son, you should now give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
So too should good sons and good daughters."
It is impossible that anyone who can receive and uphold the name of the *Baoche pusa jing* (Sūtra of the Jewel Chariot Bodhisattva) would fall into hell; there is no such case. Why is this?
Riding upon the power of the Tathāgata and embarking on the great ship of Prajñā,
they ferry sentient beings across the vast river of birth and death and reach the shore beyond the ocean of afflictions.
They emerge from the deep abyss of sensual desire;
they cross over the pits and ravines of ignorance;
they traverse the perilous path of attachment to views.
Using patience as a chisel, one hews away the stumps of the six sense bases,
exhausts the cross-roots of attachment to views,
and removes the leaves and fibers of the afflictions.
Harnessing the great ox of the vast vow,
using wisdom as a sharp plow,
one breaks through the wasteland of sentient beings' ignorance.
Using sympathetic joy as the tool for carving,
one shatters the dense forest of sentient beings' ignorance;
using the six perfections as seeds.
One scatters [offerings] upon the boundless field of merit,
using the ten wholesome actions as irrigation channels to nurture the long-standing crops of truth.
He whets the sharp sickle of Prajñā;
he gathers the true fruit of Nirvāṇa;
and he leads the great ox of the vast vows.
He drives the precious chariot of the Three Vehicles,
directing it with the compass and ruler of the Six Supernatural Powers,
along the official highway of the Eightfold Path.
The conch-shell of the dhāraṇī is the vessel that governs fortune;
it is the site of practice where accumulation is gathered and dispersed like clouds.
Such is the method by which the precious chariot delivers sentient beings.
Like a mother who contracts the illness of her son, one kills living beings to seek out demon-spirits;
yet not a single word of merit is gained, while the weight of sin is as vast as Mount Sumeru. When one contemplates the time of human aging and decay, a hundred ailments arise simultaneously;
like water being extinguished by fire, the wind of the sword dissolves the physical form, the bones separate, and the tendons and veins snap.
The great life-span must surely decline; it is for fear of this that I seek the Way and pray for the arising of merit.
Contemplating only old age, sickness, and death, I see that the three realms are a great affliction. When merit is exhausted, life comes to an end;
one is cast into the Yellow Springs, the body decays and returns to the earth, while the soul follows according to causes and conditions.
Fearing this, I therefore seek the Path and the supreme Nirvana. When the eyes grow old, they cannot see forms; it is difficult to read the words of the sutras.
When the ears grow old, they cannot hear sounds; it is difficult to listen to and receive the Dharma.
When the nose grows old, it cannot smell fragrances; it is also difficult to discern scents. When the mouth grows old, it can no longer speak.
To explain the meaning of the sutras is difficult; as the mind grows old, it forgets much. To preach the Dharma and understand its meaning is difficult;
as the body grows old, one cannot practice. To go forth and acquire merit is difficult; having failed to receive the precepts in this life, it is difficult to become a human again in the next.
Killing brings the retribution of a short life; thus, it is difficult to seek long life.
Though I have killed and returned it to me, it is still difficult to escape by fleeing;
The foolish people of the world do not believe in the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra*, Indulging themselves and attached to the five desires, they are dragged along by their own karma,
Like a horse being led for training that looks up at the blue clouds, Yet performs only the deeds that lead to hell.
Not knowing that rebirth in heaven depends on mindfulness, the wise delight in merit.
The fool seeks only to nourish his own body, like a horse greedy for water and grain; he does not listen to well-spoken verses.
Wandering through the cauldrons of boiling brine, his suffering is beyond description. Speak these words to those in my household: "I wish to transcend this state."
By burning incense and inviting practitioners of the Way, one shall not undergo the sufferings of the eight difficulties. All things are straight because the precious carriage is straight;
though the body may be crooked, the shadow remains straight. It is difficult for a crooked mind to achieve straightness in affairs;
when the mind is crooked, straightening affairs is difficult. Fish and turtles hide in the sea, yet it is difficult to seek a livelihood by sweeping the ground.
When a monkey is in haste, it clings to a tree; without a tree, even its escape is difficult. When a person is in haste, they rely upon the Buddha;
without precepts, it is difficult to seek the Buddha. If one lets the body go and gives rein to its own indulgence, the various Māras will vie to come before them.
Thus spoke the Bhikṣu to Ratnavāhana.
"Why did you not ask the Buddha about the Four Noble Truths, or from where these two causal conditions originally arise?
The Buddha then said to Ratnavāhana, "I emerged at Vārāṇasī."
Either the fruit arises from the cause,
or the cause emerges from the fruit;
the wise can establish this, but the foolish cannot.
He then dug up the precious chariot and skillfully asked how to break three things into one.
The bhikṣu said to the precious chariot,
"If you raise your mind, it should be for the great child."
This means that you followers of the three vehicles do not recognize that within the cycle of saṃsāra and the six realms of rebirth,
even to escape various hardships is difficult;
therefore, I pray that you will use the power of skillful means to lead them into nirvāṇa.
The bhikṣu spoke to Ratnavāhana:
"The matter is likewise unknowable;
from the grain of millet, heaven and earth were formed."
A mustard seed becomes Mount Sumeru;
such is the power of spiritual transformation.
Therefore, it is called "inconceivable."
The Bodhisattva Ratratha and his retinue of thousands of myriads of koṭis,
having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly;
with single-minded devotion they turned toward him, free from all doubt.
In the past, when the Buddha was in the world,
he manifested as a wandering ascetic and went to the house of a great Brahmin to beg for alms.
The brāhmaṇa asked the practitioner,
"Why do you not engage in farming but instead wander for alms?
What is your clan name and what is your personal name?"
"Where is your residence?
To which commandery and county do you belong?
The practitioner replied:
My residence is located east of Hongshui and west of Yinshui,
in Benji County of Zhuopu Commandery.
My surname is Kong and my given name is Wuxiang.

The Brahmin said, "A practitioner of the Way possesses such accomplishments as these. He had been dwelling beneath the tree of *sarvajña* (all-knowledge), having transcended entry into cities and severed all worldly ties.
The Brahmin remarked, "A man of the Way indeed possesses such deeds."
"Why do you not engage in farming but instead practice begging for food?
The practitioner replied,
"My farming is different from yours."
Taking the four dhyānas as the plow and the six pāramitās as the seeds,
they are sown across the boundless wilderness.
Moisten it with the waters of the eight liberations;
nurture it so that the four fruits may grow as its retribution;
and weed it with the ten wholesome paths as its ditches and embankments.
Furthermore, using the sharp sickle of *prajñā* as the blade and binding it with the essential attachment of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*),
one loads it upon the great carriage of the Three Vehicles.
It conveys them to the great city of the Infinite and bestows [its benefits] upon all worthy persons;
the cultivation of this field by this poor monk is thus inexhaustible.
As the practitioner was speaking these words, he suddenly vanished.
The Brahmin immediately attained the fruit of the Path.
This is the *Sūtra on the Exquisite and Beautiful Jewel Chariot*, one fascicle, translated in the thirteenth year of the Daye era.

The Buddha’s disciple Zhang Fuguo, for the sake of his virtuous friend and spiritual mentor Liu Shizhang, respectfully produced one fascicle of the *Baoche jing* (Sutra of the Precious Chariot) for circulation, recitation, exposition, and practice.

May we, by virtue of this work of propagating the Mahāyāna, travel together through sublime realms and tread upon the wondrous traces; may we turn our backs on the eightfold path of evil and return to the eightfold noble path, endowed with the power of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
Having attained the merit of the four bases of mindfulness,

I vow that throughout immeasurable kalpas in the future, in every birth and lifetime, I shall together with my disciples deeply establish roots of goodness as a bodhi-retinue, resolve upon the Mahāyāna, and seek the Mahāyāna.
Fully endowed with wisdom, supernormal powers, majestic virtue, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment, they have all achieved perfection;
together they cultivate the holy life and ascend equally to the various levels of awakening.
